summary: A 1979 specification of the Internet Message Protocol, a proposal for how messages are moved between hosts. It was written by Jon Postel and is part of the early work on internet mail. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: A set of rules for passing messages from one computer to another across connected networks.

subtitle: Protocol for routing and delivering messages across interconnected networks

tldr.problem: Individual networks have their own local message systems, but there is no standard way to route messages between different networks and systems across the internet.
tldr.mechanism: Messages are transmitted between Message Processing Modules (MPMs) in a structured format with typed data elements, including identification, command, and document parts. MPMs use routing tables and relay messages toward their destination network, with conversion between local and internet formats at network boundaries.
tldr.outcome: A unified framework allows message systems running on different networks to interoperate and exchange messages reliably.

facts.label: Data element types
facts.value: 8 types (NOP, PAD, BOOLEAN, INDEX, INTEGER, BITSTR, TEXT, LIST, PROPLIST)

today: RFC 753 specified the Internet Message Protocol in March 1979 as part of early work on internetwork mail. The specific format and control messages have been superseded by the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) and MIME, but the fundamental concepts of structured message format and inter-network message relay remain central to modern email systems.

sections.title: Internet Message Protocol
sections.content:
RFC 753 describes the Internet Message Protocol (IMP), a specification for routing and delivering messages across interconnected networks. Written by Jon Postel at ISI, the protocol addresses the challenge of letting different networks, each with their own message system, exchange messages with each other.

The model is straightforward: Message Processing Modules (MPMs) are processes running on hosts that handle message transmission. An MPM can route messages locally (to another user on the same host), to another host on the local network, or to a user on a remote network by relaying the message through one or more intermediate MPMs.

Messages are represented in a highly structured format with typed data elements, allowing them to carry not only text but also drawings, facsimile images, and digitized speech. The protocol provides a common framework for moving messages between systems, regardless of the local formats those systems use internally.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers on different networks need a common way to send messages to each other. This protocol lets a message travel from one network to another until it reaches its destination.

sections.title: Message Structure and Data Elements
sections.content:
A message comprises three parts: identification (a transaction number and the sender's internet host number), command (routing information, destination mailbox, and a list of MPMs that have handled the message), and document (a header and body containing the actual message content).

The protocol defines a rich set of typed data elements for encoding information: booleans (1/0), 16-bit and 32-bit integers, bit strings, text strings (ASCII), lists (nested structures), and property lists (name-value pairs). This structure allows the protocol to carry diverse information: addresses, dates, error messages, and binary data segments.

The MPM does not depend on understanding the document body—the delivery system treats it opaquely. This separation allows local message systems to define their own document formats while using the internet protocol for transit.
sections.plainLanguage: A message has three parts: who sent it and what number it is, where it should go and who has touched it, and the actual content. Each part is built from typed building blocks like numbers, text, and lists.

sections.title: Routing, Relaying, and Format Conversion
sections.content:
Each MPM maintains routing tables to determine which link to use for each destination. If the destination is local, the message is placed in a shared data structure for the user's interface program. For a remote destination, the MPM transmits the message to another MPM on the same network or, if the destination is on a different network, to a gateway or relay MPM.

When a message crosses from one network to another, it may need format conversion. An MPM at a network boundary can convert between the local message system's format and the internet format. Information may be lost or rephrased during conversion: a message with mixed text and speech traveling into a text-only network might replace the speech with the note "There was some speech here."

The protocol uses a reliable communication service, such as TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), for the actual data transfer between MPMs. The MPM uses commands and replies to communicate control information and to report delivery status or errors.
sections.plainLanguage: An MPM looks at the destination and either hands the message to a local user, sends it to another MPM on the same network, or sends it toward a different network. If the formats are different, some information might need to be translated or simplified.

sections.title: Design Principles and Flexibility
sections.content:
The protocol is designed with several key principles. First, it assumes little about local network addressing, since different networks use different addressing schemes. Each MPM needs to know only the addressing format of its own network and must be able to select an output link for messages destined to other networks.

Second, each MPM has a unique internet address to place a handling stamp on messages that pass through it, enabling loop detection and message tracking.

Third, the protocol is flexible about what data types messages carry and what local systems do with them. The internet format supports text, binary data, drawings, and other media, but local systems can ignore unsupported media types during conversion.

The specification provides the information needed for compatible implementations to exchange messages, while leaving room for different MPMs to make different implementation choices suited to their networks and systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol is designed to work even though networks are different, addresses are different, and some computers understand features others do not. It lets different systems cooperate by providing a common language.
